content: Personnel should be provided with comprehensive educational materials and strongly encouraged to receive the vaccine, with particular emphasis on vaccinating those who care for high-risk individuals. This includes staff in intensive care units (e.g., neonatal intensive care units), medical/surgical units, and employees of nursing homes and chronic-care facilities. To improve vaccination compliance, strategies such as using mobile carts to deliver vaccines directly to hospital wards or other work sites, and offering vaccines during night and weekend shifts, should be implemented. Additionally, a follow-up campaign may be necessary if an influenza outbreak occurs in the community. The antiviral agents with specific activity against influenza A viruses include amantadine hydrochloride and rimantadine hydrochloride. In the United States, only amantadine is licensed for use. These drugs, which are chemically related, interfere with the replication cycle of type A influenza viruses but not type B. The exact mechanisms of their antiviral activity remain incompletely understood. When administered prophylactically to healthy young adults or children before and during an epidemic, amantadine is approximately 70%-90% effective in preventing illnesses caused by naturally occurring strains of type A influenza viruses. When given within 48 hours of symptom onset for symptomatic treatment in otherwise healthy young adults and children, amantadine has been shown to reduce the duration of fever and other systemic symptoms, potentially allowing for a quicker return to normal daily activities. It is important to note that while antiviral agents taken prophylactically may prevent illness, they do not prevent subclinical infections. Consequently, individuals taking these drugs may still develop immune responses that protect them against antigenically related viruses in subsequent years. As with all medications, side effects may occur with amantadine, though they are rarely severe. However, they may be significant for certain patient populations. In the event of influenza A outbreaks in institutions housing high-risk individuals, chemoprophylaxis should be initiated as early as possible to limit the spread of infection. This may involve preapproved medication orders or plans to obtain physicians' orders on short notice. When used for outbreak control, amantadine should be administered to all residents of the affected institution, regardless of whether they received the influenza vaccine the previous fall. Dosages should be determined based on the recommendations and precautions outlined in the manufacturer's package insert and this document. To minimize the spread of the virus and reduce disruptions in patient care, chemoprophylaxis should also be offered to unvaccinated staff who provide care to high-risk individuals. For prophylaxis to be fully effective, the antiviral drug must be taken daily for the duration of influenza activity in the community. High-risk individuals can still be vaccinated after an influenza A outbreak has begun in the community. However, since the development of antibodies in adults following vaccination typically takes two weeks, amantadine should be administered during this period. Children receiving the influenza vaccine for the first time may require up to six weeks of prophylaxis or until two weeks after the second vaccine dose. Amantadine does not interfere with the antibody response to the vaccine. Chemoprophylaxis should be considered for unvaccinated individuals who frequently interact with high-risk persons in home settings (e.g., household members, visiting nurses, volunteer workers) and unvaccinated employees of hospitals, clinics, and chronic-care facilities. For employees unable to be vaccinated, chemoprophylaxis should continue for the entire period influenza A virus is circulating in the community. For those vaccinated during a time of active influenza A circulation, chemoprophylaxis should be administered for two weeks post-vaccination. Prophylaxis should also be considered for all employees, regardless of vaccination status, if the outbreak is caused by a variant strain of influenza A not covered by the vaccine. Chemoprophylaxis may be indicated for high-risk individuals expected to have a poor antibody response to the influenza vaccine, such as many individuals with HIV infection, particularly those with advanced disease. There is no available data on potential interactions with other drugs used in managing HIV-infected patients, so close monitoring is required if amantadine is used. For high-risk individuals for whom the influenza vaccine is contraindicated due to anaphylactic hypersensitivity to egg protein, chemoprophylaxis throughout the influenza season may be appropriate. Amantadine can also be used prophylactically by anyone wishing to avoid influenza A illness, with the decision made on an individual basis between the physician and patient. Although amantadine can reduce the severity and duration of influenza A illness among healthy adults, there is no evidence of its efficacy in preventing complications of influenza A among high-risk individuals. Therefore, no specific recommendations can be made regarding its therapeutic use for these patients. However, this does not preclude the use of amantadine for high-risk patients who develop influenza-like illness during periods of known or suspected influenza A activity in the community. The effectiveness of amantadine when treatment begins beyond the first 48 hours of illness is unknown. When administered to healthy young adults at a dose of 200 mg/day, minor central nervous system (CNS) side effects (e.g., nervousness, anxiety, insomnia, difficulty concentrating, and lightheadedness) and/or gastrointestinal side effects (e.g., anorexia and nausea) occur in approximately 5%-10% of patients. These side effects typically diminish or cease shortly after discontinuing the drug. With prolonged use, side effects may also diminish or disappear after the first week of use. More serious but less frequent CNS-related side effects (e.g., seizures, confusion) have primarily affected elderly individuals, those with renal disease, and those with seizure disorders or other altered mental/behavioral conditions. Reducing the dosage to ≤100 mg/day appears to lower the frequency of these side effects in such individuals without compromising the prophylactic effectiveness of amantadine. The package insert should be consulted before using amantadine for any patient. Factors such as the patient’s age, weight, renal function, presence of other medical conditions, and the indication for amantadine use (prophylaxis or therapy) must be considered, and the dosage and duration of use should be adjusted accordingly.
